bib.title: Predictability and Surprise in Large Generative Models
bib.venue: 2022 ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency (FAccT '22)

read.skipped: Reference list skimmed only for lineage.

question: How does the combination of predictable aggregate loss scaling and unpredictable specific capabilities, inputs and outputs shape the development, deployment and harms of large generative models?
hypothesis: Large generative models combine high predictability (loss follows scaling laws) with high unpredictability (specific capabilities, inputs, outputs); the former drives rapid development and the latter makes deployment consequences hard to anticipate.
contributions: Thesis with four distinguishing features: smooth general capability scaling, abrupt specific capability scaling, open-ended inputs and domains, open-ended outputs
Two novel experiments (COMPAS recidivism prediction with LMs, toxicity vs scale) plus a zero-shot recommendation experiment
Analysis of motivations and barriers to developing large models, including industry vs academia compute gap
List of policy and technical interventions

method.summary: Position paper with small original experiments on Anthropic's GPT-3-like language models of various sizes (up to 52B): few-shot recidivism prediction on COMPAS, toxicity of generations on RealToxicityPrompts, zero-shot movie rating prediction on MovieLens 1M, plus a compute-trend analysis. Other evidence is re-plotted from GPT-3, Gopher and Google program synthesis papers.
method.task: Scaling behaviour and societal-risk case studies of large language models

datasets.name: ProPublica COMPAS
datasets.split: same filtering as ProPublica notebook; 50 random labelled training examples used as few-shot (<1% of data); rest as test

datasets.name: RealToxicityPrompts
datasets.size: 1K random prompts, equal toxic and non-toxic
datasets.preprocessing: prompt labelled toxic if toxicity score >0.5

datasets.name: MovieLens 1M
datasets.size: ~4K movies, ~6K users, 1M ratings (1-5); ~160 ratings per user, 96% missing
datasets.split: 1% of dataset (10K ratings) as test set
datasets.preprocessing: up to 500 previously rated movies randomly sampled per user

other.sizes_not_listed: individual model sizes are only shown on figure axes
other.axis_range: read from Figs 3, 5, 8: roughly 1e7 to 1e10 parameters

other.note: open-source, used instead of Perspective API

inference.decoding: No sampling for COMPAS and MovieLens: next-token probabilities read directly (Yes/No normalised; ratings 1-5 normalised and probability-weighted mean)
inference.samples: Toxicity: 25 responses per prompt, 1K prompts; COMPAS and MovieLens: single probability readout per item
inference.prompting: COMPAS: few-shot with 50 random labelled examples; MovieLens: zero-shot (few-shot tested and found worse); prompts in prompts field

metrics.name: Accuracy
metrics.definition: Probability of Yes compared to ground-truth re-offence label

metrics.name: Black-to-white false positive rate ratio
metrics.definition: FPR for Black defendants divided by FPR for white defendants (Fairlearn); 1 is fair

metrics.name: Predictive accuracy ratio
metrics.definition: Accuracy Black over white; 1 is fair

metrics.name: Toxicity effect size
metrics.definition: Coefficient on model-size category in linear regression of Detoxify score on model size and prompt toxicity, with 95% CI

metrics.name: RMSE
metrics.definition: Root mean squared error between predicted and actual ratings on test set

eval.protocol: Single run per model size; no seeds stated; confidence intervals only for toxicity regression.

results.claim: Three-digit addition jumps from under 1% below 6B parameters to 80% at GPT-3 175B.
results.setup: GPT-3 family, 3-digit addition, accuracy vs parameters; figure from Brown et al.
results.quote: jumps to 8% accuracy on a 13B parameter model and 80% accuracy on a 175B parameter model

results.claim: Gopher stays under 30% on MMLU for all models under 6B, then reaches 60% at 280B.
results.setup: Gopher family, MMLU, accuracy vs parameters (chance 25%)
results.quote: the full 280B parameter Gopher model achieves 60% accuracy

results.claim: Google program synthesis models solve 6% to 13% of problems going from 68B to 138B parameters, after little change over two orders of magnitude.
results.setup: Google LMs, program synthesis, % samples solving task
results.quote: jumps substantially from 6% to 13% when the model size increases by ∼2x from 68B to 138B parameters

results.claim: In the recidivism experiment the largest LM (52B) reaches 63% accuracy versus 66% for COMPAS, with no significant difference whether race is in the prompt.
results.setup: Anthropic LMs up to 52B, few-shot (50 labelled examples), ProPublica COMPAS data (>7,000 defendants); probability of Yes normalised against No; metrics via Fairlearn
results.quote: the largest model, with 52B parameters, achieves 63% accuracy compared to COMPAS’s 66% accuracy

results.claim: False positive rate ratio (Black to white) for COMPAS is 1.92 (fair = 1).
Largest LM with race excluded from the prompt reaches a false positive rate ratio of 1.5, rising smoothly from about 12B parameters.
results.setup: 52B LM, few-shot, race excluded from prompt
results.quote: reaches a value of 1.5 for the largest model when race is excluded in the prompt

results.claim: Largest LM with race included in the prompt reaches an FPR ratio of 2.21, worse than COMPAS's 1.92, though absolute FPRs are lower (30% Black, 12.6% white vs 45% and 24%).
results.quote: a value of 2.21 when race is included in the prompt
results.note: Footnote 10 gives absolute FPRs: LM 30% Black / 12.6% white; COMPAS 45% / 24%.

results.claim: Toxicity of generated text increases smoothly with model size.
results.setup: RealToxicityPrompts, 1K prompts (half toxic), 25 samples per prompt, Detoxify scorer, linear regression on model-size categories controlling for prompt toxicity; effect size roughly 0.02 to 0.06 read from Fig 5
results.quote:
the toxicity (defined as rude, disrespectful, or unreasonable language [29])11 of text generated from language models [3]
increases smoothly and significantly with model size

results.claim: Zero-shot LMs on MovieLens 1M: smallest model RMSE 1.06 versus random 1.91; largest LM 0.94 beats the popularity baseline (0.98) but not SOTA (0.82).
results.setup: MovieLens 1M, 1% test set (10K ratings), zero-shot prompt with up to 500 sampled rated movies, expected rating from next-token probabilities over 1-5
results.quote: the largest model achieves a significantly lower RMSE (0.94) than a strong baseline model (RMSE 0.98, see below for further details)
results.note: Smallest model RMSE 1.06, random 1.91, SOTA 0.822 (0.82 in the paragraph above).

results.claim: Extrapolating the RMSE trend, an LM would reach SOTA zero-shot recommendation at about 800T parameters.
results.setup: Extrapolation of Fig 8 power-law-like trend; the authors call it incredulous
results.quote:
at 800T parameters, a language model
will achieve state of the art performance with zero-shot learning

results.claim: Compute for large-scale AI experiments has increased more than 300,000X relative to a decade ago, with the academic share falling.
results.source: OpenAI AI and Compute and Sevilla et al. data [70]
results.setup: Compute data from OpenAI AI and Compute plus additional experiments [70]; industry/academia labelled by first-author affiliation; LOWESS fit
results.quote: has increased by more than 300, 000X relative to a decade ago

results.claim: Training frontier generative models such as GPT-3 costs on the order of a million to ten million dollars.
results.setup: Authors' estimate used in policy argument; GPT-3 elsewhere said to cost several million dollars [50]
results.quote: costs on the order of a million to ten million dollars

results.claim: Scaling laws give smooth power-law test loss improvement with compute, data and parameters, while specific tasks can change abruptly; the paper's thesis.
results.setup: Argument from prior literature (Kaplan et al. 2020 Fig 1) and the examples above

limits: Authors concede many fairness metrics exist and one algorithm cannot satisfy all; COMPAS benchmark data has measurement biases.
Comparisons to proprietary COMPAS are hard to make precise.
Toxicity: effect-size magnitude vs human perception unclear; automated detectors biased; Detoxify used rather than Perspective API.
Compute analysis data are incomplete with sampling bias; no industrial production compute.
Scaling extrapolation to 800T parameters for MovieLens is described as incredulous; algorithmic improvement could shift curves.
Model sizes, architecture, training data, context length and decoding for the Anthropic models are not given here (refers to Askell et al. 2021); single run per size.
Only three abrupt-scaling examples, all taken from other papers; no systematic estimate of how common abrupt jumps are (authors say anecdotally a minority of tasks).
Pre-dates Chinchilla-style compute-optimal scaling and later work questioning whether emergence is a metric artifact; 'emergent' framing here is not tested against metric choice.

terms.definition: First, the training (and test) loss improves predictably with scale on a broad data distribution. Second, this improvement in loss tends to correlate on average with increased performance on a number of downstream tasks.
performance on a specific task can sometimes emerge quite unpredictably and abruptly at scale
